name: Adenosine (topical hair)

lead: Topical adenosine is an ingredient in hair-growth cosmetics, used by people hoping to thicken thinning hair.

It acts on dermal papilla cells, the follicle's signalling centre: a 2012 study in cultured mouse whisker follicles found it raised FGF-2 and FGF-7, stimulated dermal papilla growth and lengthened the growth phase. A 2024 paper found the androgen receptor pathway to be a candidate target, separate from minoxidil's mechanism. The work is laboratory-based.

paras: It is applied to the scalp as a leave-on serum or tonic in a daily routine, and is sometimes used next to other hair treatments. Hair changes are generally judged over months.
It is sold as a cosmetic ingredient, and safety data were not covered in the sources reviewed. Human trial results for this use were not found.

web.title: Szendzielorz & Spiewak 2025, adenosine in topical hair-loss preparations (Biomolecules)

angle.text: Topical adenosine is used for thicker-looking hair: it acts on dermal papilla cells and lengthens the growth phase in lab studies. The research so far is in cultured cells and follicles.

lead: Topical adenosine is a naturally occurring nucleoside used as an active ingredient in lotions and shampoos for thinning hair. People apply it to the scalp with the aim of thicker hair shafts, less shedding and denser-looking hair, which improves the appearance of the hairline and crown.[1][2]

In the lab, adenosine acts on dermal papilla cells, the signalling center of the follicle. A 2012 organ-culture study of mouse whisker follicles found that it stimulated dermal papilla growth and lengthened the anagen (growth) phase by raising cysteine levels through fibroblast growth factors 2 and 7.[3] A 2024 paper compared adenosine's gene-expression effects with those of minoxidil and identified the androgen receptor pathway as a candidate target.[2]

A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis by Szendzielorz and Spiewak in Biomolecules identified seven clinical trials of topical adenosine, most using a 0.75 percent lotion, in men and women with hair loss. The authors reported that adenosine appears to thicken hair, while describing the trial base as small and often industry-funded.[1]
infobox: A2B receptor, cAMP, FGF-7 and Wnt signalling in dermal papilla cells; possible androgen receptor pathway effect[1][2]

paras: Adenosine appears in hair-growth lotions and in shampoos combined with caffeine. Reviews of the topical hair-growth market list many cosmeceutical actives marketed through social media, and note that most have been studied as combined formulations with limited sample sizes.[4]

In the mouse follicle culture, adenosine increased the expression of FGF-2 and FGF-7 in dermal papilla cells and extended anagen.[3] The 2025 review describes a pathway in which adenosine binds A2B receptors on dermal papilla cells, raising cAMP and FGF-7 expression and activating Wnt/beta-catenin signalling; the authors also note that minoxidil's effects may be partly mediated by adenosine.[1]

The 2024 paper reports that an adenosine complex altered gene expression in dermal papilla cells differently from minoxidil, with inhibition of androgen receptor signalling as a candidate mechanism.[2]

The 2025 systematic review found seven trials: a 2008 double-blind placebo-controlled trial in 30 women with female pattern hair loss; a 2013 randomized comparison with 5 percent minoxidil in 110 men; a 2015 double-blind trial against 0.1 percent niacinamide in 102 men; a 2016 placebo-controlled trial in 38 men; a 2018 open-label study of a multi-ingredient lotion; and 2024 trials of a caffeine-adenosine shampoo and of an adenosine, panthenol and niacinamide complex compared with 5 percent minoxidil.[1]

A pooled analysis of three placebo-type-controlled trials of the 0.75 percent lotion at 6 months did not reach statistical significance for hair density or for thick or thin hair counts, although the authors treated the niacinamide comparator as an inactive control and concluded that adenosine appears to increase hair thickness.[1] A randomized trial of a shampoo containing caffeine and adenosine was published in the Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology in 2024.[5] A broader 2024 systematic review of androgenetic alopecia treatments covers topical, oral and procedural options.[6]

Only one of the seven trials reported adverse effects in detail: in the 2013 comparison, 3.8 percent of adenosine users reported folliculitis or itching versus 9.8 percent of minoxidil users reporting hair casts or increased shedding, a difference that was not statistically significant. A shampoo trial noted dry hair in some users.[1] The review states that the FDA and EMA have approved topical adenosine for skin application at concentrations up to 0.1 percent.[1]
